disagreement_queue.title: Cannabidiol may prevent the development of congestive hepatopathy secondary to right ventricular hypertrophy associated with pulmonary hypertension in rats
disagreement_queue.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Pulmonary hypertension (PH) can cause right ventricular (RV) failure and subsequent cardiohepatic syndrome referred to as congestive hepatopathy (CH). Passive blood stasis in the liver can affect inflammation, fibrosis, and ultimately cirrhosis. Cannabidiol (CBD) has many beneficial properties including anti-inflammatory and reduces RV systolic pressure and RV hypertrophy in monocrotaline (MCT)-induced PH in rats. Thus, it suggests that CBD may have the potential to limit CH development secondary to RV failure. The present study aimed to determine whether chronic administration of CBD can inhibit the CH secondary to RV hypertrophy associated with MCT-induced PH.

METHODS: The experiments involved rats with and without MCT-induced PH. CBD (10 mg/kg) or its vehicle was administered once daily for 3 weeks after MCT injection (60 mg/kg).

RESULTS: Monocrotaline administration increased the liver/body weight ratio. In histology examinations, we observed necrosis and vacuolar degeneration of hepatocytes as well as sinusoidal congestion. In biochemical studies, we observed increased levels of nuclear factor-κappa B (NF-κB), tumour necrosis factor-alpha (TNA-α), interleukin 1 beta (IL-1β), and interleukin 6 (IL-6). CBD administration to PH rats reduced the liver/body weight ratio, improved the architecture of the liver, and inhibited the formation of necrosis. Cannabidiol also decreased the level of NF-κB, TNF-α, IL-1β and IL-6.

CONCLUSIONS: The studies show that CBD can protect the liver from CH probably through attenuating PH, protective effects on the RV, and possibly direct anti-inflammatory effects on liver tissue through regulation of the NF-κB pathway.

disagreement_queue.title: Cannabidiol improves muscular lipid profile by affecting the expression of fatty acid transporters and inhibiting de novo lipogenesis

Two-week CBD administration significantly reduced the intramuscular fatty acids (FAs) accumulation and inhibited de novo lipogenesis in different lipid pools (in the free fatty acid, diacylglycerol, and triacylglycerol fractions) in both muscle types, which coincided with a decrease in the expression of membrane fatty acid transporters (fatty acid translocase, membrane-associated fatty acid binding protein, and fatty acid transport proteins 1 and 4). Moreover, CBD application profoundly improved the elongation and desaturation ratios, which was in line with downregulated expression of enzymes from the family of elongases and desaturases regardless of the metabolism presented by the muscle type. To our knowledge, this study is the first that outlines the novel effects of CBD action on skeletal muscle with different types of metabolism (oxidative vs. glycolytic).

disagreement_queue.title: Effects of chronic cannabidiol in a mouse model of naturally occurring neuroinflammation, neurodegeneration, and spontaneous seizures
disagreement_queue.abstract: Cannabidiol (CBD) has gained attention as a therapeutic agent and is purported to have immunomodulatory, neuroprotective, and anti-seizure effects. Here, we determined the effects of chronic CBD administration in a mouse model of CLN1 disease (Cln1-/-) that simultaneously exhibits neuroinflammation, neurodegeneration, and spontaneous seizures. Proteomic analysis showed that putative CBD receptors are expressed at similar levels in the brains of Cln1-/- mice compared to normal animals. Cln1-/- mice received an oral dose (100 mg/kg/day) of CBD for six months and were evaluated for changes in pathological markers of disease and seizures. Chronic cannabidiol administration was well-tolerated, high levels of CBD were detected in the brain, and markers of astrocytosis and microgliosis were reduced. However, CBD had no apparent effect on seizure frequency or neuron survival. These data are consistent with CBD having immunomodulatory effects. disagreement_queue.title: THC and CBD affect metabolic syndrome parameters including microbiome in mice fed high fat-cholesterol diet
disagreement_queue.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) is associated with metabolic syndrome, which often includes obesity, diabetes, and dyslipidemia. Several studies in mice and humans have implicated the involvement of the gut microbiome in NAFLD. While cannabis and its phytocannabinoids may potentially be beneficial for treating metabolic disorders such as NAFLD, their effects on liver diseases and gut microbiota profile have yet to be addressed. In this study, we evaluated the therapeutic effects of the two major cannabinoids, delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) and cannabidiol (CBD), on NAFLD progression.

METHODS: NAFLD was induced by feeding mice a high fat-cholesterol diet (HFCD) for 6 weeks. During this period, the individual cannabinoids, THC or CBD, were added to the experimental diets at a concentration of 2.5 or 2.39 mg/kg. Profile of lipids, liver enzymes, glucose tolerance, and gene expression related to carbohydrate lipids metabolism and liver inflammation was analyzed. The effect of THC or CBD on microbiota composition in the gut was evaluated.

RESULTS: While not alleviating hepatic steatosis, THC or CBD treatment influenced a number of parameters in the HFCD mouse model. CBD increased food intake, improved glucose tolerance, reduced some of the inflammatory response including TNFa and iNOS, and partially mitigated the microbiome dysbiosis observed in the HFCD fed mice. THC produced a much weaker response, only slightly reducing inflammatory-related gene expression and microbiome dysbiosis.

CONCLUSIONS: The results of this study indicate the potential therapeutic effects of individual phytocannabinoids are different from the effects of the cannabis plant possessing a mixture of compounds. While CBD may help ameliorate symptoms of NAFLD, THC alone may not be as effective. This disparity can putatively be explained based on changes in the gut microbiota.

disagreement_queue.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a chronic autoimmune disease of the central nervous system characterized by neuroinflammation, demyelination and axonal loss. Cannabis, an immunomodulating agent, is known for its ability to treat MS effectively. However, due to variations in the profile of secondary metabolites, especially cannabinoids, among cannabis cultivars, the effectiveness of cannabis treatment can vary, with significant variability in the effects on different biological parameters. For screening available cultivars, cellular in vitro as well as pre-clinical in vivo assays, are required to evaluate the effectiveness of the wide range of chemical variability that exists in cannabis cultivars. This study evaluated comparatively three chemically diverse cannabis cultivars, CN2, CN4 and CN6, containing different ratios of phytocannabinoids, for their neuroinflammatory activity in MS model.

MATERIALS AND METHODS: In vitro experiments were performed with lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-activated BV-2 microglia and primary glial cells to evaluate the effect of different cannabis cultivars on nitric oxide (NO) and inflammatory cytokines, as well as inducible nitric oxide synthase (iNOS) protein expression. An in vivo experiment using the experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE) MS model was conducted using Myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein (MOG) as the activating peptide. The cannabis extracts of the cultivars CN2, CN4, CN6 or vehicle, were intraperitoneally injected with clinical scores given based on observed symptoms over the course of study. At the end of the experiment, the mice were sacrificed, and splenocyte cytokine secretion was measured using ELISA. Lumbar sections from the spinal cord of treated MS mice were evaluated for microglia, astrocytes and CD4+ cells.

All extracts were not cytotoxic in glial cells up to 50 µg/ml. Dose dependent inhibition of LPS-induced BV2 as well as primary microglial NO secretion confirmed the anti-inflammatory and anti-oxidative activity of the three cannabis cultivars. CN2 but not CN4 reduced both astrocytosis and microglial activation in lumbar sections of EAE mice. In contrast, CN4 but not CN2 significantly decreased the secretion of TNFα and Interferon γ (IFNγ) in primary splenocytes extracted from EAE mice.

disagreement_queue.title: Cannabis Sativa targets mediobasal hypothalamic neurons to stimulate appetite
disagreement_queue.abstract: The neurobiological mechanisms that regulate the appetite-stimulatory properties of cannabis sativa are unresolved. This work examined the hypothesis that cannabinoid-1 receptor (CB1R) expressing neurons in the mediobasal hypothalamus (MBH) regulate increased appetite following cannabis vapor inhalation. Here we utilized a paradigm where vaporized cannabis plant matter was administered passively to rodents. Initial studies in rats characterized meal patterns and operant responding for palatable food following exposure to air or vapor cannabis. Studies conducted in mice used a combination of in vivo optical imaging, electrophysiology and chemogenetic manipulations to determine the importance of MBH neurons for cannabis-induced feeding behavior. Our data indicate that cannabis vapor increased meal frequency and food seeking behavior without altering locomotor activity. Importantly, we observed augmented MBH activity within distinct neuronal populations when mice anticipated or consumed food. Mechanistic experiments demonstrated that pharmacological activation of CB1R attenuated inhibitory synaptic tone onto hunger promoting Agouti Related Peptide (AgRP) neurons within the MBH. Lastly, chemogenetic inhibition of AgRP neurons attenuated the appetite promoting effects of cannabis vapor. Based on these results, we conclude that MBH neurons contribute to the appetite stimulatory properties of inhaled cannabis.

disagreement_queue.title: GPR55 is expressed in glutamate neurons and functionally modulates nicotine taking and seeking in rats and mice
disagreement_queue.abstract: Cannabis legalization continues to progress in the USA for medical and recreational purposes. G protein-coupled receptor 55 (GPR55) is a putative "CB3" receptor. However, its functional role in cannabinoid action and drug abuse is not explored. Here we report that GPR55 is mainly expressed in cortical and subcortical glutamate neurons and its activation attenuates nicotine taking and seeking in rats and mice. RNAscope in situ hybridization detected GPR55 mRNA in cortical vesicular glutamate transporter 1 (VgluT1)-positive and subcortical VgluT2-positive glutamate neurons in wildtype, but not GPR55-knockout, mice. GPR55 mRNA was not detected in midbrain dopamine (DA) neurons in either genotype. Immunohistochemistry assays detected GPR55-like staining, but the signal is not GPR55-specific as the immunostaining was still detectable in GPR55-knockout mice. We then used a fluorescent CB1-GPR55 ligand (T1117) and detected GPR55 binding in cortical and subcortical glutamate neurons, but not in midbrain DA neurons, in CB1-knockout mice. Systemic administration of O-1602, a GPR55 agonist, dose-dependently increased extracellular glutamate, not DA, in the nucleus accumbens. Pretreatment with O-1602 failed to alter Δ9-tetrahydrocannabinol (D9-THC)-induced triad effects or intravenous cocaine self-administration, but it dose-dependently inhibited nicotine self-administration under fixed-ratio and progressive-ratio reinforcement schedules in rats and wildtype mice, not in GPR55-knockout mice. O-1602 itself is not rewarding or aversive as assessed by optical intracranial self-stimulation (oICSS) in DAT-Cre mice. These findings suggest that GPR55 is functionally involved in nicotine reward process possibly by a glutamate-dependent mechanism, and therefore, GPR55 deserves further research as a new therapeutic target for treating nicotine use disorder.

disagreement_queue.title: Trema micranthum (L.) Blume as a new source of cannabinoids
disagreement_queue.abstract: Trema micranthum (Cannabaceae) has emerged as a promising new source of cannabinoids, including cannabidiol (CBD). Given the substantial medicinal demand for cannabinoids and the regulatory challenges associated with Cannabis sativa due to the presence of Δ9-tetrahydrocannabinol (THC), this study sought to explore the presence of CBD, THC, and their precursors, Δ9-tetrahydrocannabinolic acid A (THCA A) and cannabidiolic acid (CBDA), in various parts of Trema micranthum using UHPLC-HRMS/MS (Orbitrap). Extracts from fruits, leaves, inflorescences, and stems were obtained using a methanol/hexane (9:1, v/v) solvent mixture. UHPLC coupled with an Orbitrap mass spectrometer was employed for cannabinoid identification and quantification, with standard mixtures prepared in methanol. The extracts yielded significant quantities, such as 6.6%/g from leaves and 3%/g from fruits. Cannabinoids were detected in fruits, leaves, and inflorescences, with acidic forms (CBDA and THCA A) present in higher concentrations than their neutral counterparts. Notably, leaves contained 4.43 × 10-3 µg/g of CBD and 1.05 ×  10-3 µg/g of THC. These findings, facilitated by high-resolution analytical methods, underscore the potential of Trema micranthum as an alternative source for cannabinoids, guiding future research in this area.

disagreement_queue.title: Cannabinoid combination targets NOTCH1-mutated T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia through the integrated stress response pathway
disagreement_queue.abstract: In T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (T-ALL), more than 50% of cases display autoactivation of Notch1 signaling, leading to oncogenic transformation. We have previously identified a specific chemovar of Cannabis that induces apoptosis by preventing Notch1 maturation in leukemia cells. Here, we isolated three cannabinoids from this chemovar that synergistically mimic the effects of the whole extract. Two were previously known, cannabidiol (CBD) and cannabidivarin (CBDV), whereas the third cannabinoid, which we termed 331-18A, was identified and fully characterized in this study. We demonstrated that these cannabinoids act through cannabinoid receptor type 2 and TRPV1 to activate the integrated stress response pathway by depleting intracellular Ca2+. This is followed by increased mRNA and protein expression of ATF4, CHOP, and CHAC1, which is hindered by inhibiting the upstream initiation factor eIF2α. The increased abundance of CHAC1 prevents Notch1 maturation, thereby reducing the levels of the active Notch1 intracellular domain, and consequently decreasing cell viability and increasing apoptosis. Treatment with the three isolated molecules resulted in reduced tumor size and weight in vivo and slowed leukemia progression in mice models. Altogether, this study elucidated the mechanism of action of three distinct cannabinoids in modulating the Notch1 pathway, and constitutes an important step in the establishment of a new therapy for treating NOTCH1-mutated diseases and cancers such as T-ALL.

disagreement_queue.title: Comparing CB1 receptor GIRK channel responses to receptor internalization using a kinetic imaging assay
disagreement_queue.abstract: The type 1 cannabinoid receptor (CB1R) mediates neurotransmitter release and synaptic plasticity in the central nervous system. Endogenous, plant-derived, synthetic cannabinoids bind to CB1R, initiating the inhibitory G-protein (Gi) and the β-arrestin signaling pathways. Within the Gi signaling pathway, CB1R activates G protein-gated, inwardly-rectifying potassium (GIRK) channels. The β-arrestin pathway reduces CB1R expression on the cell surface through receptor internalization. Because of their association with analgesia and drug tolerance, GIRK channels and receptor internalization are of interest to the development of pharmaceuticals. This research used immortalized mouse pituitary gland cells transduced with a pH-sensitive, fluorescently-tagged human CB1R (AtT20-SEPCB1) to measure GIRK channel activity and CB1R internalization. Cannabinoid-induced GIRK channel activity is measured by using a fluorescent membrane-potential sensitive dye. We developed a kinetic imaging assay that visualizes and measures CB1R internalization. All cannabinoids stimulated a GIRK channel response with a rank order potency of WIN55,212-2 > (±)CP55,940 > Δ9-THC > AEA. Efficacy was expressed relative to (±)CP55,940 with a rank order efficacy of (±)CP55,940 > WIN55, 212-2 > AEA > Δ9-THC. All cannabinoids stimulated CB1R internalization with a rank order potency of (±)CP55,940 > WIN55, 212-2 > AEA > Δ9-THC. Internalization efficacy was normalized to (±)CP55,940 with a rank order efficacy of WIN55,212-2 > AEA > (±)CP55,940 > Δ9-THC. (±)CP55,940 was significantly more potent and efficacious than AEA and Δ9-THC at stimulating a GIRK channel response; no significant differences between potency and efficacy were observed with CB1R internalization. No significant differences were found when comparing a cannabinoid's GIRK channel and CB1R internalization response. In conclusion, AtT20-SEPCB1 cells can be used to assess cannabinoid-induced CB1R internalization. While cannabinoids display differential Gi signaling when compared to each other, this did not extend to CB1R internalization.

disagreement_queue.title: Cannabidivarin and cannabigerol induce unfolded protein response and angiogenesis dysregulation in placental trophoblast HTR-8/SVneo cells
disagreement_queue.abstract: Cannabidivarin (CBDV) and cannabigerol (CBG) are minor phytocannabinoids from Cannabis sativa, whose health benefits have been reported. However, studies about the impact of these cannabinoids on fundamental cellular processes in placentation are scarce. Placental development involves physiological endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress, however when exacerbated it can lead to altered angiogenesis and pregnancy disorders, such as intrauterine growth restriction and preeclampsia. In this work, the effects of CBDV and CBG (1-10 µM) on placental extravillous trophoblasts were studied, using the in vitro model HTR-8/SVneo cells. Both cannabinoids induced anti-proliferative effects and reactive oxygen/nitrogen species generation, which was dependent on transient receptor potential vanilloid 1 (TRPV1) activation. Moreover, CBDV and CBG significantly upregulated, in a TRPV-1 dependent manner, the gene expression of HSPA5/Glucose-regulated protein 78 (GRP78/BiP), a critical chaperone involved in ER stress and unfolded protein response (UPR) activation. Nevertheless, the UPR pathways were differentially activated. Both cannabinoids were able to recruit the IRE branch, while only CBDV enhanced the expression of downstream effectors of the PERK pathway, namely p-eIF2α, ATF4 and CHOP. It also augmented the activity of the apoptotic initiator caspases-8 and -9, though the effector caspases-3/-7 were not activated. TRB3 expression was increased by CBDV, which may hinder apoptosis termination. Moreover, both compounds upregulated the mRNA levels of the angiogenic factors VEGFA, PGF and sFLT1, and disrupted the endothelial-like behavior of HTR-8/SVneo cells, by reducing tube formation. Thus, CBDV and CBG treatment interferes with EVTs functions and may have a negative impact in placentation and in pregnancy outcome.

disagreement_queue.title: Toxicity of cannabidiol and its metabolites in TM3 mouse Leydig cells: a comparison with primary human Leydig cells
disagreement_queue.abstract: Cannabidiol (CBD), one of the major components extracted from the plant Cannabis sativa L., has been used as a prescription drug to treat seizures in many countries. CBD-induced male reproductive toxicity has been reported in animal models; however, the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. We previously reported that CBD induced apoptosis in primary human Leydig cells, which constitute the primary steroidogenic cell population in the testicular interstitium. In this study, we investigated the effects of CBD and its metabolites on TM3 mouse Leydig cells. CBD, at concentrations below 30 µM, reduced cell viability, induced G1 cell cycle arrest, and inhibited DNA synthesis. CBD induced apoptosis after exposure to high concentrations (≥ 50 µM) for 24 h or a low concentration (20 µM) for 6 days. 7-Hydroxy-CBD and 7-carboxy-CBD, the main CBD metabolites of CBD, exhibited the similar toxic effects as CBD. In addition, we conducted a time-course mRNA-sequencing analysis in both primary human Leydig cells and TM3 mouse Leydig cells to understand and compare the mechanisms underlying CBD-induced cytotoxicity. mRNA-sequencing analysis of CBD-treated human and mouse Leydig cells over a 5-day time-course indicated similar responses in both cell types. Mitochondria and lysosome dysfunction, oxidative stress, and autophagy were the major enriched pathways in both cell types. Taken together, these findings demonstrate comparable toxic effects and underlying mechanisms in CBD-treated mouse and primary human Leydig cells.

disagreement_queue.abstract: The potentially adverse effects of cannabis (marijuana), a common leisure compound, on male reproductive performance are a reason for concern. δ-9-tetrahydrocannabinol (THC), the primary active component of marijuana alters testicular cells' proliferation and function which affects male fertility and causes testicular cells dysfunction and apoptosis. The main objective of this study was to investigate the possible mechanism underlying the toxic effects of THC with a mechanistic insight into Sertoli cell-based reproductive dysfunction. The Mus musculus Sertoli cell line (TM4) was cultured and exposed to different concentrations of THC and, MTT (3-(4, 5-Dimethylthiazol-2-yl)-2,5-diphenyltetrazolium bromide) assay was then performed for evaluating cell viability. The expression of caspase-3 gene and genes related to growth factors were analyzed by real-time RT-PCR. Western blotting was performed for evaluating protein expression level. Moreover, caspase-3 mRNA expression levels significantly increased while growth factors mRNA levels decreased in THC-exposed cells compared to unexposed cells. disagreement_queue.title: Microglial cannabinoid receptor type 1 mediates social memory deficits in mice produced by adolescent THC exposure and 16p11.2 duplication
disagreement_queue.abstract: Adolescent cannabis use increases the risk for cognitive impairments and psychiatric disorders. Cannabinoid receptor type 1 (Cnr1) is expressed not only in neurons and astrocytes, but also in microglia, which shape synaptic connections during adolescence. However, the role of microglia in mediating the adverse cognitive effects of delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol (THC), the principal psychoactive constituent of cannabis, is not fully understood. Here, we report that in mice, adolescent THC exposure produces microglial apoptosis in the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC), which was exacerbated in a model of 16p11.2 duplication, a representative copy number variation (CNV) risk factor for psychiatric disorders. These effects are mediated by microglial Cnr1, leading to reduction in the excitability of mPFC pyramidal-tract neurons and deficits in social memory in adulthood. Our findings suggest the microglial Cnr1 may contribute to adverse effect of cannabis exposure in genetically vulnerable individuals.

disagreement_queue.title: Cannabidiol inhibits Nav channels through two distinct binding sites
disagreement_queue.abstract: Cannabidiol (CBD), a major non-psychoactive phytocannabinoid in cannabis, is an effective treatment for some forms of epilepsy and pain. At high concentrations, CBD interacts with a huge variety of proteins, but which targets are most relevant for clinical actions is still unclear. Here we show that CBD interacts with Nav1.7 channels at sub-micromolar concentrations in a state-dependent manner. Electrophysiological experiments show that CBD binds to the inactivated state of Nav1.7 channels with a dissociation constant of about 50 nM. The cryo-EM structure of CBD bound to Nav1.7 channels reveals two distinct binding sites. One is in the IV-I fenestration near the upper pore. The other binding site is directly next to the inactivated "wedged" position of the Ile/Phe/Met (IFM) motif on the short linker between repeats III and IV, which mediates fast inactivation. Consistent with producing a direct stabilization of the inactivated state, mutating residues in this binding site greatly reduced state-dependent binding of CBD. The identification of this binding site may enable design of compounds with improved properties compared to CBD itself.

disagreement_queue.title: Characterization of cannabis strain-plant-derived extracellular vesicles as potential biomarkers
disagreement_queue.abstract: The scientific interest in cannabis plants' beneficial properties has recently sparked certain interest in the possible functional characterization of plant-derived extracellular vesicles (PDEVs). Establishing the most appropriate and efficient isolation procedure for PDEVs remains a challenge due to vast differences in the physio-structural characteristics of different plants within the same genera and species. In this study, we employed a crude but standard isolation procedure for the extraction of apoplastic wash fluid (AWF) which is known to contain the PDEVs. This method includes a detailed stepwise process of PDEV extraction from five (5) cultivars of cannabis plants, namely: Citrus (C), Henola (HA), Bialobrezenski (BZ), Southern-Sunset (SS), and Cat-Daddy (CAD). Approximately, 150 leaves were collected from each plant strain. In order to collect PDEV pellets, apoplastic wash fluid (AWF) was extracted from plants via negative pressure permeabilization and infiltration followed by high-speed differential ultracentrifugation. Particle tracking analysis of PDEVs revealed particle size distribution in the range of 20 to 200 nm from all plant strains, while PDEV total protein concentration from HA was higher than that of SS. Although HA-PDEVs' total protein was higher than SS-PDEVs, SS-PDEVs' RNA yield was higher than that of HA-PDEVs. Our result suggests that the cannabis plant strains contain EVs, and PDEV concentration from the cannabis plant could be age or strain dependent. Overall, the results provide a guide for the selection and optimization of PDEV isolation methods for future studies.

maude_improvement_brief.summary: Node2c suffers from four systemic extraction failures. First, treatment_duration is null in 85% of papers because the extractor lacks regex patterns for in-vitro incubation phrases, simulation runtimes, and storage durations. Second, strain_reported captures downstream reagent vendor strings (Sigma-Aldrich catalog codes) rather than cultivar names or compound identifiers because no blocklist or priority ranking exists. Third, outcome_domain defaults to 'other' instead of oncology, pain, or addiction because the keyword dictionary omits cell-biology terms like 'apoptosis', 'glioblastoma', 'GIRK', and 'drug tolerance'. Fourth, study_type and thc_pct/cbd_pct are mis-classified because analytical chemistry papers (HPLC, UHPLC, docking) are incorrectly routed through the clinical branch, and percentage extractors capture acid-fraction ratios instead of plant-content values. Fixing the four extractor functions and adding a pre-routing guard for analytical methods will close the majority of the 26.5-point alignment gap.

maude_improvement_brief.agent_handoff_prompt:
CANNABIS PAPER SCRAPER - NODE2C IMPLEMENTATION BRIEF
Alignment baseline: 75.4% | Target: >90%
Files in scope: extractor.py, maude_classifier.py, maude_cues.json

---

OVERVIEW

Four gap patterns account for the bulk of alignment loss in node2c. In order of impact: study_type misrouting of analytical and computational papers (60% disagreement), strain_reported capturing vendor strings (90% disagreement), treatment_duration returning null for in-vitro durations (85% disagreement), and outcome_domain defaulting to other when cell-biology oncology or pain terms are present (45% disagreement). Two additional medium-priority improvements cover cannabinoid percentage context guards and cannabis_type isolate classification. All changes are self-contained within the three named files.

---

SECTION 1: extractor.py CHANGES

1A. extract_treatment_duration() - In-vitro time pattern expansion

Current behavior: The function regex-matches human dosing schedules and clinical time windows. It misses in-vitro incubation periods, molecular dynamics simulation lengths, and cold-storage durations that appear in cell biology and analytical papers.

Implementation steps:

Add a second pattern list specifically for in-vitro and computational contexts. Insert this before the fallback return so that if the primary (clinical) pattern list returns nothing, the function proceeds to try the in-vitro list.

Primary in-vitro patterns to add (compile with re.IGNORECASE):

  r'incubated?\s+for\s+([\d.]+\s*(?:h(?:ours?)?|min(?:utes?)?|days?))'
  r'treated?\s+for\s+([\d.]+\s*(?:h(?:ours?)?|min(?:utes?)?|days?))'
  r'([\d.]+)\s*ns\s+(?:MD|molecular dynamics|simulation)'
  r'simulation\s+(?:of|for|totaling)\s+([\d.]+\s*(?:ns|us|microseconds?))'
  r'stored?\s+for\s+([\d]+)\s*days?'
  r'([\d]+)[- ]day\s+(?:storage|stability|shelf)'

Scope guard: Before attempting in-vitro patterns, verify that the text block being searched is tagged or contextually associated with Methods or Results. If section tagging is not available, check that the 30-character left-context of any match does not contain clinical scheduling language such as "weeks treatment" or "daily dose" to avoid false positives in mixed papers.

Preference rule: When multiple in-vitro duration matches exist, prefer the shortest numeric value on the assumption that it represents the acute incubation window rather than a cell-maintenance or storage period. Implement by collecting all matches from the in-vitro list, converting to a common unit (hours), sorting ascending, and returning the first.

Return format: Keep consistent with existing function output. Append unit string to the numeric value (e.g., "24 h", "100 ns"). Do not strip units as downstream consumers rely on them for normalization.

1B. extract_strain_reported() - Vendor blocklist and cultivar prioritization

Current behavior: Token-level matching picks up vendor names and catalog strings such as "Sigma-Aldrich" or "Cayman Chemical" and returns them as the strain value.

Implementation steps:

Define a module-level constant VENDOR_BLOCKLIST as a list of lowercase patterns:
  ["sigma", "aldrich", "tocris", "cayman", "abcam", "santa cruz", "millipore",
   "catalog no", "cat no", "cat #", r'[a-z]{1,3}\d{4,}', "lot no", "item no",
   "selleckchem", "apexbio", "biolegend"]

The final pattern in that list catches alphanumeric catalog codes like "C7522" or "THC-001".

Before returning any candidate token, iterate through VENDOR_BLOCKLIST. If any pattern matches (case-insensitive substring or regex match), remove that candidate from consideration.

Add a prioritized positive-match list checked before the main extraction loop. Patterns in priority order:

  1. r'cv\.\s*([\w ]+)'  (cultivar abbreviation common in botany papers)
  2. r'chemovar\s+([\w -]+)'
  3. r'chemotype\s+([IVX]+)'
  4. Named isolate match: compound name appears in CANNABINOID_ISOLATE_LIST (defined in 1E below)
  5. Strain name following "strain", "variety", "cultivar" keyword

If a prioritized match is found, return it immediately without running the general token scan.

Only if the full candidate list is empty after blocklist filtering should the function fall back to returning the best available token, including a vendor string, to avoid returning None where something is better than nothing.

1C. extract_cannabinoid_pct() - Context guard for acid-fraction values

Current behavior: The function captures numeric percentages without verifying whether they describe plant-level weight-percent or acidic-form ratios. Acid-form ratios can exceed 50 and are not comparable to plant-content defaults.

Implementation steps:

After capturing a numeric value from the existing regex, extract the surrounding window of plus-or-minus 30 characters from the source string.

Check the window (lowercased) for any of: "acid", "acidic", "ratio", "acid to total", "thca", "cbda". If any are found, discard this match and continue searching.

Add a range validation step after the context check:
  - For THC, accept values only in range 0.0 to 40.0 (plant-content ceiling)
  - For CBD, accept values only in range 0.0 to 25.0

Values above these ceilings that are not already discarded by the acid context guard should be flagged with a warning log line but not returned as the primary value. If no value passes both guards, return None rather than a likely-incorrect high value.

This guard should wrap both thc_pct and cbd_pct extraction paths since the same acid-ratio contamination occurs in both.

1D. OUTCOME_DOMAIN_KEYWORDS dictionary expansion

Locate the OUTCOME_DOMAIN_KEYWORDS dictionary (or equivalent structure) in extractor.py. Append the following terms to the listed sublists:

Oncology sublist additions:
  "leukemia", "glioblastoma", "T-ALL", "lymphoma", "tumor cell",
  "apoptosis in", "cytotoxicity", "antiproliferative", "cell viability",
  "IC50", "MTT assay", "colony formation"

Pain sublist additions:
  "GIRK", "analgesia", "analgesic", "nociception", "hyperalgesia",
  "allodynia", "pain threshold"

Addiction sublist additions:
  "drug tolerance", "receptor internalization", "desensitization",
  "withdrawal", "conditioned place preference", "CPP"

After appending, ensure matching is case-insensitive (either lowercase all text before comparison or use re.IGNORECASE flags). The IC50 and MTT additions are particularly important for cell-biology papers that dominate the node2c gap.

1E. extract_cannabis_type() - Isolate detection before fallback

Define module-level constant CANNABINOID_ISOLATE_LIST:
  ["THC", "CBD", "CBDV", "THCV", "CBG", "CBGA", "CBCA", "CBC",
   "delta-9-THC", "delta-8-THC", "cannabidiol", "cannabigerol",
   "tetrahydrocannabivarin", "cannabidivarin", "dronabinol", "nabilone",
   "JWH-018", "WIN 55,212", "HU-210", "CP 55,940", "anandamide", "AEA",
   "2-AG", "2-arachidonoylglycerol"]

In extract_cannabis_type(), before the existing logic runs the fallback or concentrate-detection path, add an isolate check:

  1. Tokenize or scan the abstract and methods text for any member of CANNABINOID_ISOLATE_LIST (case-insensitive, whole-word or dash-adjacent match to avoid catching "CBD" inside "CBDA").
  2. If a match is found, check that neither "extract", "oil", "flower", "plant material", "crude", nor "tincture" appears within 50 characters of the match.
  3. If the isolate is confirmed without a plant-matrix context word, return "pure cannabinoid".
  4. Otherwise continue to existing logic.

This prevents concentrates or unknown from being returned for papers that use a single synthetic or isolated compound in cell culture.

---

SECTION 2: maude_classifier.py CHANGES

2A. study_type - Analytical and computational pre-routing guard

This is the highest-impact single fix. The clinical routing branch is being reached by papers about HPLC method development, HRMS identification studies, and molecular dynamics simulations, which share surface language with observational studies (e.g., "patients" mentioned in introduction, "reported" outcomes).

Add a pre-check function called is_analytical_or_computational(text) that returns True if any of the following terms appear (case-insensitive, whole-word):

  ["UHPLC", "HPLC", "HRMS", "Orbitrap", "LC-MS", "GC-MS", "mass spectrometry",
   "molecular docking", "molecular dynamics", "GROMACS", "AutoDock", "Vina",
   "DFT", "density functional", "in silico", "docking score", "binding affinity",

SECTION 1: extractor.py CHANGES

1A. extract_treatment_duration() - In-vitro time pattern expansion

Current behavior: The function regex-matches human dosing schedules and clinical time windows. It misses in-vitro incubation periods, molecular dynamics simulation lengths, and cold-storage durations that appear in cell biology and analytical papers.

Implementation steps:

Add a second pattern list specifically for in-vitro and computational contexts. Insert this before the fallback return so that if the primary (clinical) pattern list returns nothing, the function proceeds to try the in-vitro list.

Primary in-vitro patterns to add (compile with re.IGNORECASE):

  r'incubated?\s+for\s+([\d.]+\s*(?:h(?:ours?)?|min(?:utes?)?|days?))'
  r'treated?\s+for\s+([\d.]+\s*(?:h(?:ours?)?|min(?:utes?)?|days?))'
  r'([\d.]+)\s*ns\s+(?:MD|molecular dynamics|simulation)'
  r'simulation\s+(?:of|for|totaling)\s+([\d.]+\s*(?:ns|us|microseconds?))'
  r'stored?\s+for\s+([\d]+)\s*days?'
  r'([\d]+)[- ]day\s+(?:storage|stability|shelf)'

Scope guard: Before attempting in-vitro patterns, verify that the text block being searched is tagged or contextually associated with Methods or Results. If section tagging is not available, check that the 30-character left-context of any match does not contain clinical scheduling language such as "weeks treatment" or "daily dose" to avoid false positives in mixed papers.

Preference rule: When multiple in-vitro duration matches exist, prefer the shortest numeric value on the assumption that it represents the acute incubation window rather than a cell-maintenance or storage period. Implement by collecting all matches from the in-vitro list, converting to a common unit (hours), sorting ascending, and returning the first.

Return format: Keep consistent with existing function output. Append unit string to the numeric value (e.g., "24 h", "100 ns"). Do not strip units as downstream consumers rely on them for normalization.

1B. extract_strain_reported() - Vendor blocklist and cultivar prioritization

Current behavior: Token-level matching picks up vendor names and catalog strings such as "Sigma-Aldrich" or "Cayman Chemical" and returns them as the strain value.

Implementation steps:

Define a module-level constant VENDOR_BLOCKLIST as a list of lowercase patterns:
  ["sigma", "aldrich", "tocris", "cayman", "abcam", "santa cruz", "millipore",
   "catalog no", "cat no", "cat #", r'[a-z]{1,3}\d{4,}', "lot no", "item no",
   "selleckchem", "apexbio", "biolegend"]

The final pattern in that list catches alphanumeric catalog codes like "C7522" or "THC-001".

Before returning any candidate token, iterate through VENDOR_BLOCKLIST. If any pattern matches (case-insensitive substring or regex match), remove that candidate from consideration.

Add a prioritized positive-match list checked before the main extraction loop. Patterns in priority order:

  1. r'cv\.\s*([\w ]+)'  (cultivar abbreviation common in botany papers)
  2. r'chemovar\s+([\w -]+)'
  3. r'chemotype\s+([IVX]+)'
  4. Named isolate match: compound name appears in CANNABINOID_ISOLATE_LIST (defined in 1E below)
  5. Strain name following "strain", "variety", "cultivar" keyword

If a prioritized match is found, return it immediately without running the general token scan.

Only if the full candidate list is empty after blocklist filtering should the function fall back to returning the best available token, including a vendor string, to avoid returning None where something is better than nothing.

1C. extract_cannabinoid_pct() - Context guard for acid-fraction values

Current behavior: The function captures numeric percentages without verifying whether they describe plant-level weight-percent or acidic-form ratios. Acid-form ratios can exceed 50 and are not comparable to plant-content defaults.

Implementation steps:

After capturing a numeric value from the existing regex, extract the surrounding window of plus-or-minus 30 characters from the source string.

Check the window (lowercased) for any of: "acid", "acidic", "ratio", "acid to total", "thca", "cbda". If any are found, discard this match and continue searching.

Add a range validation step after the context check:
  - For THC, accept values only in range 0.0 to 40.0 (plant-content ceiling)
  - For CBD, accept values only in range 0.0 to 25.0

Values above these ceilings that are not already discarded by the acid context guard should be flagged with a warning log line but not returned as the primary value. If no value passes both guards, return None rather than a likely-incorrect high value.

This guard should wrap both thc_pct and cbd_pct extraction paths since the same acid-ratio contamination occurs in both.

After appending, ensure matching is case-insensitive (either lowercase all text before comparison or use re.IGNORECASE flags). The IC50 and MTT additions are particularly important for cell-biology papers that dominate the node2c gap.

1E. extract_cannabis_type() - Isolate detection before fallback

Define module-level constant CANNABINOID_ISOLATE_LIST:
  ["THC", "CBD", "CBDV", "THCV", "CBG", "CBGA", "CBCA", "CBC",

   "JWH-018", "WIN 55,212", "HU-210", "CP 55,940", "anandamide", "AEA",
   "2-AG", "2-arachidonoylglycerol"]

In extract_cannabis_type(), before the existing logic runs the fallback or concentrate-detection path, add an isolate check:

  1. Tokenize or scan the abstract and methods text for any member of CANNABINOID_ISOLATE_LIST (case-insensitive, whole-word or dash-adjacent match to avoid catching "CBD" inside "CBDA").
  2. If a match is found, check that neither "extract", "oil", "flower", "plant material", "crude", nor "tincture" appears within 50 characters of the match.

  4. Otherwise continue to existing logic.

OVERVIEW
─────────────────────────────────────────────

This brief covers seven rule changes derived from gap analysis showing systematic extraction failures across four categories: strain/compound provenance conflation, exposure-method misfires in ex vivo and aquatic contexts, dietary-delivery misclassification as edibles, and dose field imputation errors. All seven changes are required to move alignment above the 80% threshold. Changes are ordered high-priority first.

─────────────────────────────────────────────
CHANGE 1 — strain_reported: DUAL-TARGET EXTRACTION
File: extractor.py | Priority: HIGH
─────────────────────────────────────────────

Problem: strain_reported currently attempts one extraction pass looking for animal catalog strings (e.g., Sprague-Dawley, C57BL/6, JAX colony numbers). For pure-cannabinoid studies that source compound from a chemical vendor, the field returns null or incorrectly inherits an irrelevant string. Claude returns the compound provenance string (compound name + vendor + purity) in these cases, creating 100% disagreement on the strain_reported field for that paper subset.

Implementation:

Split the extraction function into two sequential sub-extractors operating on the full abstract and any available methods text.

Sub-extractor A — Animal strain/vendor: retain all existing patterns for JAX, Envigo, Charles River, Harlan, Taconic, and common inbred/outbred strain designators (Sprague-Dawley, Wistar, C57BL/6, BALB/c, CD-1, Long-Evans, etc.). This runs first. If a match is found, assign it and skip sub-extractor B.

Sub-extractor B — Compound provenance: activated only when (a) cannabis_type resolves to 'pure cannabinoid' AND (b) sub-extractor A returns null. Build a pattern that captures: compound name (THC, CBD, cannabidiol, delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol, CBG, CBDV, etc.) followed within 0–80 characters by any of: Sigma-Aldrich, Cayman Chemical, Tocris, NIDA Drug Supply Program, THC Pharm, Lipomed, or a purity expression (greater-than N%, NNN mg/mL, certified reference). Cannabis Paper Scraper - Node2b Implementation Brief

OVERVIEW

This brief covers eight targeted changes across extractor.py, maude_classifier.py, and maude_cues.json for the node2b sub-pipeline. The changes address four critical gap patterns: missing temporal extractors, cannabis_type misclassification, inactive strain extraction, and zero inhaled exposure duration capture. Work should be completed in roughly the order presented, since the high-priority extractor additions unblock classifier fixes that depend on richer field data.

Alignment is currently 66.7%. Expected alignment target post-implementation is 88-92% based on gap pattern frequency weights.


PART 1 - extractor.py CHANGES

1a. extract_administration_frequency()

Add a new standalone function. It should accept a text string (concatenated abstract and methods sections, lowercased). Apply re.search with the following patterns in priority order. Return the first match normalized to a short canonical string. If no match is found, return None.

Pattern list (compile once at module level as FREQ_PATTERNS):
  - r'twice daily' -> "twice daily"
  - r'once daily' -> "once daily"
  - r'\bdaily\b' -> "daily"
  - r'every other day' -> "every other day"
  - r'alternating days?' -> "alternating days"
  - r'(\d+)\s*days?\s*on[,/\s]+(\d+)\s*days?\s*off' -> "Xd on / Yd off" (format with captured groups)
  - r'twice weekly' -> "twice weekly"
  - r'\bweekly\b' -> "weekly"

The patterns must be checked in the order listed. "twice daily" must be checked before "daily" to prevent the shorter pattern swallowing the longer phrase. Return the normalized string, not the raw match.

Call site: inside the node2b field assembly block, run this against abstract_text + " " + methods_text and assign result to record["administration_frequency"].

1b. extract_duration_days()

Add a function accepting the same combined text string. Apply the following regex patterns in order, converting all results to integer days. Return an integer or None.

Pattern A: r'for\s+(\d+)\s*days?' -> return int(group 1)
Pattern B: r'over\s+(\d+)\s*weeks?' -> return int(group 1) * 7
Pattern C: r'from\s+(?:PND|postnatal day)\s*(\d+)\s+to\s+(?:PND|postnatal day)\s*(\d+)' -> return int(group 2) - int(group 1)
Pattern D: r'gestational\s+days?\s+(\d+)\s+(?:to|-)\s+(\d+)' -> return int(group 2) - int(group 1)
Pattern E: r'for\s+(\d+)\s*months?' -> return int(group 1) * 30 (approximate; flag with a comment that this is approximate)

If multiple patterns match, use the first match found. If the arithmetic result would be zero or negative (e.g., malformed text), return None rather than a nonsensical value. Assign to record["duration_days"].

1c. extract_inhaled_exposure_duration()

Add a function that returns a string like "30 minutes" or None. Regex pattern:
r'(\d+)[- ]min(?:ute)?s?\s+(?:vapor|smoke|inhalation|session)'

Capture group 1 is the number. Return "{N} minutes". This function should only be called when the exposure_method field already contains "smoke", "vapor", "vaporization", or "inhalation" (case-insensitive check on the classified value). Assign to record["inhaled_exposure_duration"].

Note for the developer: some papers state "four 30-min sessions" so the number immediately before "min" may be preceded by a hyphen or space. The current regex handles both. Do not parse the session count here; that is a separate field if needed later.

1d. extract_thc_mg_ml()

Add a function returning a float or None. Two regex patterns to try in sequence:

Pattern A: r'(\d+(?:\.\d+)?)\s*mg/m[Ll][^\n]{0,40}THC'
Pattern B: r'THC[^\n]{0,40}?(\d+(?:\.\d+)?)\s*mg/m[Ll]'

Both patterns look within 40 characters of the THC mention to avoid false positives from unrelated concentration values in the same sentence. Return float(group 1) from whichever pattern matches first. Only call this function when exposure_method is smoke or vapor. Assign to record["thc_mg_ml"].

1e. strain_reported - split into sub-extractors

Replace the existing (non-functional) strain_reported extractor with two sub-functions, then merge results.

extract_animal_strain(text):
Build a list ANIMAL_STRAIN_PATTERNS at module level. Include at minimum:
  r'\bSprague[- ]Dawley\b'
  r'\bWistar\b'
  r'\bLong[- ]Evans\b'
  r'\bC57BL/6[A-Z]?\b'
  r'\bBALB/c\b'
  r'\bCD-1\b'
  r'\bFischer 344\b'
  r'\bLewis\b' (with word boundary to avoid false matches)
Return a list of unique matched strings from re.findall across the text.

extract_cannabis_strain_or_compound(text):
Build CANNABIS_STRAIN_PATTERNS including:
  r'\bCN\d+\b' (cultivar codes like CN2, CN6)
  r'\b\d{3}-\d+[A-Z]?\b' (codes like 331-18A)
  r'\bCP-55[\s,]?940\b'
  r'\bWIN\s?55[\s,]?212\b'
  r'\bHU-210\b'
  r'\bJWH-\d+\b'
  r'\bAM-\d+\b'
Also capture vendor-context phrases: if "Sigma" or "Cayman" appears within 60 characters of "THC" or "CBD", record "isolated THC (Sigma)" or "isolated CBD (Cayman)" as appropriate using a proximity check rather than a single giant regex.

Merge step: strain_reported = extract_animal_strain(text) + extract_cannabis_strain_or_compound(text). Deduplicate. If the merged list is empty, assign None rather than an empty list to keep downstream null checks consistent.


PART 2 - maude_classifier.py CHANGES

2a. Fix cannabis_type classification

At the top of the node2b handler, define:

SYNTHETIC_CB_AGONISTS = {"cp-55940", "cp55940", "win55212", "win 55212-2", "hu-210", "hu210", "jwh-018", "am-2201"}

Classification priority order (enforce with if/elif chain, NOT a flat keyword scan):

Step 1: Lowercase the full text. If any token in SYNTHETIC_CB_AGONISTS appears, set cannabis_type = "CB receptor agonist". Break.

Step 2: If ("sigma" in text or "cayman" in text or "thc isolate" in text or "cbd isolate" in text) and ("delta-9-thc" in text or "cannabidiol" in text or isolated compound language), set cannabis_type = "pure cannabinoid". Break.

Step 3: If "nabiximols" in text or "sativex" in text, set cannabis_type = "nabiximols". Break.

Step 4: If "cannabis extract" in text or "bho" in text or "butane hash oil" in text, set cannabis_type = "cannabis extract". Break.

Step 5: If "dried flower" in text or "cannabis flower" in text or "herbal cannabis" in text, set cannabis_type = "dried flower". Break.

Step 6: If delivery context includes smoke/vapor, do NOT automatically assign "vape pen". Only assign "vape pen" if the text explicitly mentions "vape pen", "vaping device", "e-cigarette", or "cartridge". Otherwise assign "cannabis smoke" for combustion or "cannabis vapor" for vaporization. The key fix is removing the existing fallback that defaults to "vape pen" from inhalation context alone.

Step 7: Fallback -> "unknown".

2b. Fix exposure_method classification

Define at module level:
ORAL_KEYWORDS = {"edible", "food treat", "oral gavage", "by mouth", "gavage", "per os", "p.o.", "oral administration", "intragastric", "chow", "drinking water", "in food"}

In the exposure_method classifier block, check ORAL_KEYWORDS before checking inhalation keywords. The current classifier appears to reach inhalation checks first and can misclassify gavage papers that mention vaporization in the discussion. Fix by ordering: oral check -> inhalation check -> injection check -> topical check -> unknown.

For inhalation papers in small rodents (species is rat or mouse), add a default rule: if "whole-body chamber" or "whole body exposure" is NOT present in the text, default inhalation subtype to "nose-only". Expose this as exposure_method_detail field rather than overwriting exposure_method.

2c. Routing fix - node1b gate override

In the node1b routing block (before the paper is stamped as a review), add a pre-check:

If abstract contains any of ("in vivo", "in-vivo") AND any animal species term from a short list (rat, mouse, mice, rodent, rabbit, monkey, primate, zebrafish, canine) -> override route to node2b.

This check must run before the review classifier keyword check (which catches "systematic review", "meta-analysis", "review of" etc.). The current bug is that paper 7209 matched a review keyword before the in vivo override had a chance to fire. Moving the override earlier in the decision tree fixes it.

Log a warning when this override fires so reviewers can audit the affected papers: "node1b override: paper {paper_id} redirected to node2b due to in vivo signal in abstract."


PART 3 - maude_cues.json CHANGES

Add or update the following cue groups. Keep existing cues intact; these are additions.

Under "temporal_cues" (create this group if absent):
  - administration_frequency_terms: ["daily", "twice daily", "once daily", "every other day", "alternating days", "weekly", "twice weekly"]
  - duration_markers: ["for N days", "over N weeks", "PND", "postnatal day", "gestational day", "GD"]
  - session_duration_markers: ["min session", "minute session", "min vapor", "minute inhalation"]

Under "cannabis_type_cues":
  - synthetic_cb_agonists: ["CP-55940", "WIN55212", "HU-210", "JWH-018", "AM-2201"]
  - pure_cannabinoid_vendors: ["Sigma-Aldrich", "Cayman Chemical", "THC isolate", "CBD isolate", "delta-9-THC (Sigma)", "delta-9-THC (Cayman)"]
  - do_not_infer_vape: true (boolean flag read by classifier to enforce the no-fallback rule)

Under "strain_cues":
  - animal_strains: ["Sprague-Dawley", "Wistar", "Long-Evans", "C57BL/6J", "BALB/c", "Fischer 344", "CD-1", "Lewis"]
  - cannabis_cultivar_pattern: "CN\\d+|\\d{3}-\\d+[A-Z]?"
  - synthetic_compound_pattern: "CP-55940|WIN\\s?55212|HU-210|JWH-\\d+|AM-\\d+"

Under "routing_cues":
  - in_vivo_override_terms: ["in vivo", "in-vivo"]
  - animal_species_terms: ["rat", "mouse", "mice", "rodent", "rabbit", "monkey", "primate", "zebrafish", "canine", "dog"]

Note: the JSON cues serve as documentation and as source-of-truth for the MAUDE scoring model. If any cue list is updated in maude_cues.json, the corresponding Python constant in maude_classifier.py must also be updated. Consider adding a startup assertion that compares the two sources if drift has been a problem.


PART 4 - TEST IDEAS

Unit tests for extractor.py:

Test extract_administration_frequency with input "Animals were dosed twice daily for 14 days." -> expect "twice daily", not "daily".
Test with input "daily injections were given" -> expect "daily".
Test with input "doses on alternating days" -> expect "alternating days".
Test with no matching phrase -> expect None.

Test extract_duration_days with "for 28 days" -> 28.
Test with "over 3 weeks" -> 21.
Test with "from PND 4 to PND 21" -> 17.
Test with "gestational days 5 to 18" -> 13.
Test with "for 2 months" -> 60 (approximate flag).
Test with ambiguous or no duration phrase -> None.

Test extract_inhaled_exposure_duration with "four 30-min vapor sessions" -> "30 minutes".
Test with "60 minute inhalation sessions" -> "60 minutes".
Test that function returns None when exposure_method is "oral gavage".

Test extract_thc_mg_ml with "THC at 5 mg/mL was vaporized" -> 5.0.
Test with "vaporized 2.5 mg/ml THC" -> 2.5.
Test with no concentration -> None.

Test strain_reported with "Sprague-Dawley rats received CP-55940" -> list contains both "Sprague-Dawley" and "CP-55940".
Test with "C57BL/6J mice" -> list contains "C57BL/6J".
Test with "CN2 cannabis cultivar" -> list contains "CN2".

Integration tests for maude_classifier.py:

Test cannabis_type on abstract mentioning "CP-55940 (Sigma-Aldrich)" -> "CB receptor agonist", not "pure cannabinoid" and not "vape pen".
Test with abstract mentioning "delta-9-THC obtained from Cayman Chemical" and no inhalation context -> "pure cannabinoid".
Test inhalation abstract with no "vape pen" mention -> must NOT return "vape pen".
Test abstract with "whole-body vapor chamber" -> exposure_method_detail should NOT be "nose-only".
Test abstract with "vapor inhalation" in rats with no chamber type specified -> exposure_method_detail = "nose-only".
Test oral: abstract with "oral gavage" and unrelated vaporization mention in discussion -> exposure_method = "oral gavage".

Routing test:

Test paper 7209 case: abstract contains "in vivo" and "rats" but also "systematic" somewhere in title -> must route to node2b.
Test clean review paper (no in vivo, no animal species) -> routes to node1b_reviews as before.

Regression guard:
After all changes, run the existing alignment suite. If alignment drops below 66.7% on any previously-passing field, the change introduced a regression and must be reverted before merging.


IMPLEMENTATION NOTES

The eight changes are independent enough to be developed in parallel, but should be merged in two batches: (1) all extractor.py additions first, tested in isolation, then (2) maude_classifier.py and maude_cues.json updates together since the classifier reads the cue file at import time.

The inhaled_exposure_duration and thc_mg_ml functions are conditional on exposure_method, so they must be called after exposure_method is classified. Ensure the node2b handler calls classify_exposure_method before calling these two extractors.

For the strain_reported vendor proximity check, set a tolerance of 60 characters as noted. If performance is a concern on large texts, restrict the search to the first 800 characters of the methods section where vendor sourcing is typically stated.

proposed_cues.explanation: When dosing is expressed as mg/kg alongside a cannabinoid name (THC, CBD, cannabidiol, tetrahydrocannabinol) and no plant-matter language appears, this strongly signals 'pure cannabinoid'.
Pharmaceutical supplier names (Sigma-Aldrich, Cayman Chemical, Tocris) confirm isolated pure cannabinoid, not plant extract.
Phrase 'cannabinoid agonist' or 'CB1 agonist' / 'CB2 agonist' maps to 'CB receptor agonist', not 'unknown'.
Distinguishes dried flower / whole plant vapor from vape pen products; should trigger 'dried flower' classification.
Explicit label 'synthetic cannabinoid' maps to 'CB receptor agonist' category.
Word 'cultivar' or 'chemovar' adjacent to a name string signals a strain name to extract.
'isolated from [strain name]' pattern identifies the source cultivar as strain_reported.
Phrase 'twice daily' should map to administration_frequency = 'twice daily'.
Pattern 'daily from gestational day X-Y' encodes both frequency (daily) and duration (Y-X days).
Compute duration_days = Y - X when gestational day range is stated (e.g., GD 6-20 → 15 days).
Explicit 'N days' or 'N-day treatment' phrases should be parsed directly as duration_days.
'N-min sessions' or 'N minutes' in inhalation context maps to inhaled_exposure_duration.
'edible' or 'food treat' signals oral administration route.
Regex pattern 'THC\s*\(?([0-9.]+)\s*mg/kg' should extract thc_mg_kg numeric value.
Regex pattern 'CBD\s*\(?([0-9.]+)\s*mg/kg' should extract cbd_mg_kg numeric value.

The fix requires adding five new extraction functions and refactoring the cannabis_type classifier with a priority-ordered compound-type decision tree.

```
Return first match string or null.

```

handoff_learning_log.summary_title: Node 2c targeted handoff — treatment_duration + strain_reported on same holdout
learning_notes: Same 20-paper node2c holdout; focused on diverging characteristic fields only (treatment_duration 17/20 disagree, strain_reported 18/20 disagree after patch 165531).

treatment_duration replaces shortest-first with context scoring: incubation/treatment/viability windows beat prep-step minutes; 24 h preference rank resolves multi-match PDFs; MD 'simulated during N ns' and hour-to-day ranges supported; full-PDF fallback when Methods omit simulation runtime.

strain_reported adds in-vitro priority path: chemotype I/II/III profiles, cv. quoted names, 331-18A/CBDV panels, compound panels (CP55,940/WIN/AEA/SR141716), botanical alternative sources; suppresses ethics-only animal strains and bare THC/CBD vendor tokens in cell-culture context.

Greedy cultivar/variety regex and isolated-from captures tightened to block PDF noise (e.g. 'cultivar yields…', PLGA fragments); extended cultivar codes limited to 331-* series in Cannasoul purchase sentences.
classify_paper forwards full_text to extract_all_heuristics for duration/strain fallbacks beyond Methods isolation.

handoff_learning_log.summary_title: Node 2c patch 165531 — in-vitro duration, strain blocklist, analytical routing
learning_notes: First node2c RL cycle on 20 pdf_extracted in-vitro papers (75.4% alignment baseline). treatment_duration now captures incubation hours, MD simulation ns/us runtimes, and storage-day phrases — preferring the shortest acute window when multiple durations appear.

strain_reported prioritizes cv./chemovar/chemotype labels and filters reagent vendor/catalog tokens; pure-cannabinoid compound provenance still includes vendors when explicitly tagged pure cannabinoid (node2b-compatible).

Analytical/computational pre-routing guard (UHPLC, HPLC, HRMS, docking, GROMACS) forces Cell Culture (Other In Vitro) before clinical observational fallback; outcome_domain expanded for oncology cell-biology, GIRK/pain, and receptor-internalization addiction cues.
THC/CBD percent extractors reject acid-fraction ratio contexts and enforce plant-content ceilings (≤40% THC, ≤25% CBD); isolated cannabinoids without plant-matrix language map to pure cannabinoid.
Shared extractor.py changes inherit to node2a/2b where applicable; node2c-specific cues documented under extraction_cues.node2c_invitro in maude_cues.json.

handoff_learning_log.summary_title: Node 2b patch 163733 — compound provenance, exposure guards, dose parsing
learning_notes: strain_reported uses dual-target logic: animal catalog strains win when present; otherwise pure-cannabinoid papers populate compound provenance (catalog id + vendor + purity) instead of null or vendor-catalog noise.

Exposure routing checks dissolved-in-media bath/immersion cues before injection; injection only fires when explicit route abbreviations (i.p., i.v., s.c., …) appear near cannabinoid mentions — removing the injection default fallback.
cannabis_type edibles tag requires explicit product phrases; Sigma/Cayman/Tocris/NIDA/THC Pharm vendor cues override dietary delivery to pure cannabinoid.

duration_days captures following/after N days, N days of treatment, and week-to-day conversion; mg/kg/day parsing fills thc_mg_kg/cbd_mg_kg; administration_frequency no longer invents once-daily defaults (normalizes to daily).
dose_mg only accepts explicit absolute-dose phrasing — mg/kg-only papers leave dose_mg null while populating mg/kg fields.

handoff_learning_log.summary_title: Node 2b patch 154633 — temporal extractors, strain, exposure routing
learning_notes: Expanded administration_frequency and duration_days parsers: weekly/alternating/on-off schedules, explicit for-N-days, over-N-weeks, and PND/postnatal day ranges.
strain_reported now merges animal strains (Sprague-Dawley, C57BL/6J, …) with synthetic test articles (CP-55940, WIN55212, JWH/AM series) and vendor-proximate isolated THC/CBD labels.
In vivo exposure routing prefers oral/edible cues before injection; unqualified vapor/smoke in rodents defaults to nose-only rather than whole-body chamber.
Added extract_thc_mg_ml for inhalation papers and tightened inhaled session duration regex (N-min vapor/smoke/inhalation session).
node1 routing override sends in vivo + animal-species abstracts to original research before review title cues fire; maude_cues.json documents temporal/strain/routing cue groups.
Re-scored the same 20 pdf_extracted holdout papers on deployed Fly code; refresh batch calibration_20260622_161904_043 reproduced 66.2% alignment and 49.9% Maude recall — classifier output is stable.

Compared to the pre-PDF pass on identical paper IDs (153659 subset): alignment 65.0%→66.2% (+1.2pp), Maude recall 37.2%→49.9% (+12.7pp). Most recall gain came from loading full PDF Methods text, not a second code patch.
Only one Maude codebase update has been applied so far (handoff 151932 in extractor.py / maude_classifier.py / maude_cues.json). Staged patch 154633 remains unimplemented.

90% alignment gate is still not met on this holdout — next step is applying feedback patch 154633 or a new disagreement-driven handoff, then re-measuring this same paper set.

Cannabis product type now uses a priority decision tree: synthetic agonists/antagonists and pharma-isolated compounds are detected before broad labels like vape pen or unknown — and vape pen only fires on explicit device terms, not vapor inhalation alone.

Strain, dose, and schedule fields parse Methods text shared across node2a/2b/2c: cultivar codes (CN2/CN4), supplier-qualified compounds, mg/kg THC/CBD (with µg/kg conversion), gestational-day ranges, and phrases like twice daily.
Exposure route logic prefers oral/edible when food-delivery cues appear near THC/CBD mentions, so injection keywords in background text no longer override edible administration.

Adjacent node2 branches inherit the same extractor.py logic and shared extraction_cues in maude_cues.json — clinical trials and in vitro papers benefit from the same dose/duration/strain parsers without separate handoffs.
